subject: math
title: Data and Graphs: Sorting, Tally Tables, Pictographs, Line Plots and Bar Graphs
seo_title: Grade 2 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Tally Tables, Pictographs, Bar Graphs (Free, Answer Key, Ontario)
standard_text: Display sets of data, using one-to-one correspondence, in concrete graphs, pictographs, line plots, and bar graphs with proper sources, titles, and labels
meta_desc: Free Grade 2 math worksheets on data and graphs for the Ontario curriculum: sort in Venn and Carroll diagrams, two-way tally tables, pictographs and line plots, bar graphs with a scale of 1, and the mode. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: One symbol, one X or one tally mark stands for one answer. Count carefully, then compare.
key_sub: A group of tally marks is 5, not 4. In a Venn diagram, count the overlap and the things outside the circles. The mode is the answer that appears most often, not the biggest number.
body_html:
Ask, sort, count, show, explain

Data is information we collect. We can ask a question, such as “What is your favourite winter sport?”, or we can watch and count, such as birds at the feeder. Then we sort the data, count it with tally marks, show it in a graph, and say what it tells us.

Sort by two things

A Venn diagram has two circles. Things that fit both labels go in the overlap, where the circles cross. Things that fit neither label go outside the circles.

A Carroll diagram is a table of boxes. Each thing goes in the box for its row and its column.

Example

Where does a blue circle go in the Venn diagram above?

It is not red. It is not a triangle.

Answer: Outside the circles

Two-way tally tables

A two-way tally table shows two things about each person, such as their grade and their favourite snack. Make one mark for each answer. The fifth mark goes across the other four.

Pictographs and line plots

In Grade 2, one symbol or one X stands for one thing. Line the symbols up, all the same size, so the rows are easy to compare.

A line plot puts an X above a number line for each answer.

Bar graphs

A good bar graph has a title, labels, a scale and a source (where the data came from). In Grade 2 the scale counts by 1s. Go to the top of a bar, then across to the scale.

Example

How many more students chose hockey than skiing?

Hockey 7, skiing 3. 7 − 3 = 4.

Answer: 4 more students

The mode

The mode is the answer that appears most often. In a graph, it is the tallest bar or the longest row. Data can have one mode, two modes, or no mode.

Example

Goals: 2, 3, 1, 3, 2, 3. What is the mode?

3 appears three times. That is the most.

Answer: 3

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting a group of 5 tally marks as 4The line across is the 5th mark
Reading one box of a two-way table for the whole rowAdd both boxes in the row
Forgetting the overlap or the things outside the circlesCount every part of the Venn diagram
Adding the numbers under a line plotCount the X’s: each X is one answer
Giving the biggest number as the modeThe mode is the answer that appears most often
Adding when the question says how many moreHow many more means take away

faq.q: What do Grade 2 students learn about data in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They sort data by two attributes in Venn and Carroll diagrams, organize it in two-way tally tables, and show it in pictographs, line plots and bar graphs where one symbol stands for one. They also find the mode and explain what the data tells them.

faq.q: What is a two-way tally table?
faq.a: It is a tally table that shows two pieces of information at once, such as a student’s grade (columns) and favourite snack (rows). Each tally mark goes in the box where its row and column meet.

faq.q: What is the mode in Grade 2 math?
faq.a: The mode is the answer or number that appears most often. Data can have one mode, two modes (a tie), or no mode when every answer appears the same number of times.

faq.q: What is a line plot in Grade 2?
faq.a: A line plot shows data with an X above a number line for each answer, such as the number of teeth each student has lost. Count the X’s above a number to see how many students gave that answer.

sets.title: Sort by two attributes: Venn and Carroll diagrams

items.q: How many shapes are big and red?
items.e: Find the box in the Big row and the Red column. That is box A. It has 3 shapes. (7 is all the red shapes, and 5 is all the big shapes.)

items.q: How many shapes are blue?
items.e: Add both boxes in the Blue column: 2 big + 6 small. 2 + 6 = 8. (6 is only the small blue shapes.)

items.q: How many shapes are small?
items.e: Add both boxes in the Small row: 4 red + 6 blue. 4 + 6 = 10.

items.q: Which box should a small blue triangle go in?
items.e: It is small, so it goes in the Small row. It is blue, so it goes in the Blue column. That is box D. (The shape does not matter here. Only size and colour.)

items.q: Which box should a big blue star go in?
items.e: It is big: Big row. It is blue: Blue column. That is box B.

items.q: How many more small shapes are there than big shapes?
items.e: Small: 4 + 6 = 10. Big: 3 + 2 = 5. How many more means take away: 10 − 5 = 5. (15 adds them.)

items.q: How many shapes are red triangles?
items.e: Red triangles are red and triangles, so they are in the overlap, where the circles cross. There are 2. (5 counts the whole Red circle.)

items.q: How many triangles are there?
items.e: Count the whole Triangles circle, and do not forget the overlap: 4 + 2 = 6. (4 forgets the red triangles in the overlap.)

items.q: Where should a new red triangle go?
items.e: It is red and it is a triangle. It belongs in both circles, so it goes in the overlap.

items.q: Where should a blue circle go?
items.e: A blue circle is not red and not a triangle. It does not fit either circle, so it goes outside the circles.

items.q: Where should a yellow triangle go?
items.e: It is a triangle, but it is not red. It goes only in the Triangles circle, not in the overlap.

items.q: How many shapes are not red?
items.e: Shapes that are not red are outside the Red circle: 4 in the Triangles part and 4 outside both circles. 4 + 4 = 8. (4 forgets the shapes outside the circles.)

items.q: How many numbers are even and more than 50?
items.e: Numbers that fit both labels are in the overlap: 62, 96 and 70. That is 3 numbers. (7 is the whole Even circle, and 6 is the whole More than 50 circle.)

items.q: Where should 50 go?
items.e: 50 is even (it ends in 0). But 50 is not more than 50. It is equal to 50. So 50 goes only in the Even circle.

items.q: Where should 49 go?
items.e: 49 is odd (it ends in 9), so it is not even. 49 is less than 50. It fits neither circle, so it goes outside.

items.q: One number is in the wrong place. Which number is it?
items.e: 46 is even, but 46 is less than 50. It should be only in the Even circle, not in the overlap.

items.q: How many students have a dog and a cat?
items.e: Students with both pets are in the overlap: Emma and Kai. That is 2 students.

items.q: How many students have a dog?
items.e: Count the whole dog circle: Liam, Ava, Mateo, Chloe and Emma, Kai in the overlap. 4 + 2 = 6. (4 forgets the students in the overlap.)

items.q: How many students have no dog and no cat?
items.e: No dog and no cat means outside both circles: Mei, Arjun and Zoe. That is 3 students.

items.q: Hana sorts 12, 35, 40 and 7 in a Venn diagram. The circles are “Even” and “More than 30”. Which number goes in the overlap?
items.e: 40 is even, and 40 is more than 30, so it goes in the overlap. 35 is more than 30 but odd. 12 is even but not more than 30. 7 goes outside both circles.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: The fifth mark goes across the other four, so each group is 5. 1 group of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, then 6, 7. So it is 7.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: The fifth mark goes across the other four, so each group is 5. 2 groups of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, 10, then 11, 12. So it is 12.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: The fifth mark goes across the other four, so each group is 5. 3 groups of 5. Count 5, 10, 15. So it is 15.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: The fifth mark goes across the other four, so each group is 5. 3 groups of 5 and 3 more. Count 5, 10, 15, then 16, 17, 18. So it is 18.
13 = 5 + 5 + 3. Look for 2 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is B. A shows 18 (one group too many), C shows 12 (one mark missing), D shows 14 (one mark too many).

items.q: How many Grade 2 students chose cheese?
items.e: Find the Cheese row and the Grade 2 column. 1 group of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So it is 9. (3 is the Grade 1 box. 12 adds both grades.)

items.q: How many students chose apples?
items.e: Add both boxes in the Apples row: Grade 1 has 6 and Grade 2 has 5. 6 + 5 = 11. (6 or 5 reads only one box.)

items.q: How many Grade 1 students answered the survey?
items.e: Add every box in the Grade 1 column: 6 + 3 + 8 + 4 = 21. (19 counts each group of 5 as 4. 25 is the Grade 2 column.)

items.q: Which snack did the most Grade 2 students choose?
items.e: Look only at the Grade 2 column: apples 5, cheese 9, crackers 4, yogurt 7. Cheese has the most. (Crackers is the most in Grade 1.)

items.q: How many more Grade 1 students than Grade 2 students chose crackers?
items.e: Crackers: Grade 1 has 8 and Grade 2 has 4. How many more means take away: 8 − 4 = 4. (12 adds them.)

items.q: How many students answered altogether?
items.e: Grade 1: 21. Grade 2: 5 + 9 + 4 + 7 = 25. Altogether: 21 + 25 = 46. (41 counts each group of 5 tally marks as 4.)

items.q: This table shows two things about each student. What are they?
items.e: Each tally mark is in a row (the snack) and a column (the grade). So the table shows each student’s grade and favourite snack.

items.q: One more Grade 2 student chooses yogurt. Where does the new tally mark go?
items.e: Find the Yogurt row. Then go across to the Grade 2 column. Add one mark there.

items.q: How many students wear mitts?
items.e: Add the Mitts row: Grade 1 has 14 and Grade 2 has 8. 14 + 8 = 22. (20 counts each group of 5 as 4. 16 is the Gloves row.)

items.q: Which sentence is true?
items.e: Grade 2: gloves 11 and mitts 8. 11 is more than 8, so this is true. In Grade 1, mitts (14) is more than gloves (5). Mitts 22 is more than gloves 16. Grade 2 has 8 + 11 = 19 students.

items.q: How many fewer Grade 1 students wear gloves than mitts?
items.e: Grade 1: mitts 14, gloves 5. How many fewer means take away: 14 − 5 = 9. (19 adds them. 11 is the Grade 2 box.)

items.q: Owen says these tally marks show 11. They show 13. What did he do wrong?
items.e: Each group has 4 lines and 1 line across, so it is 5. Owen counted 4 + 4 + 3 = 11. The right way: 5 + 5 + 3 = 13.

items.q: Sofia counts 14 votes for hockey. How should she draw the tally marks?
items.e: 14 = 5 + 5 + 4. Draw 2 groups of 5 and 4 single marks. When you get to the fifth mark, draw it across the other four.

items.q: A two-way tally table shows that 9 Grade 1 students and 7 Grade 2 students like hockey. 6 Grade 1 students and 8 Grade 2 students like skating. How many students like skating?
items.e: Skating: 6 in Grade 1 and 8 in Grade 2. 6 + 8 = 14. (16 is the hockey row.)

items.q: Use the same table: 9 Grade 1 and 7 Grade 2 students like hockey, and 6 Grade 1 and 8 Grade 2 students like skating. How many Grade 2 students are in the table?
items.e: Grade 2: 7 like hockey and 8 like skating. 7 + 8 = 15. (16 and 14 add a row, not the Grade 2 column.)
Each star = 1 student. Touch each star in the Fall row and count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. So 5 students.
The stars line up, so the longest row has the most. Summer has 9 stars.
Count the stars in each row: winter 6, spring 4, summer 9, fall 5. Winter has 6.
Summer 9, spring 4. How many more means take away: 9 − 4 = 5. (13 adds them.)
Add every row: 6 + 4 + 9 + 5 = 24. (4 is the number of rows, not students.)

items.q: How many fewer blue jays than juncos did the class see?
items.e: Juncos 8, blue jays 3. How many fewer means take away: 8 − 3 = 5. (11 adds them.)

items.q: How many chickadees and cardinals did the class see altogether?
items.e: Chickadees 7, cardinals 5. Altogether means add: 7 + 5 = 12. (2 takes away.)

items.q: The class saw 6 sparrows. How many circles should go in a new Sparrow row?
items.e: The key says each circle = 1 bird. 6 sparrows need 6 circles, one for each bird.

items.q: Which sport got more votes?
items.e: Count, do not look at the length. Hockey has 5 circles and skating has 7. The hockey row looks longer only because its circles are big and far apart. In a good pictograph, all symbols are the same size and line up.

items.q: Leah makes a pictograph. 5 students chose skating, but the Skating row has 4 stars. What should she do?
items.e: Each star stands for 1 student, so 5 students need 5 stars. 5 − 4 = 1. She needs 1 more star.

items.q: How many students have lost 3 teeth?
items.e: Find 3 on the number line. Count the X’s above it: 5. Each X is 1 student. (3 is the number of teeth, not the number of students.)

items.q: How many students are shown on the line plot?
items.e: Each X is one student. Count all the X’s: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 21. (15 adds the numbers 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 under the line.)

items.q: How many students have lost more than 3 teeth?
items.e: More than 3 means 4 or 5 teeth: 3 + 1 = 4 students. Do not count the students above 3. (9 adds the 5 students who lost exactly 3.)

items.q: What number of teeth lost is the most common?
items.e: The tallest stack of X’s is above 2. It has 6 X’s. So 2 teeth is the most common. (6 is how many students, and 5 is the biggest number on the line.)

items.q: How many students have 2 pets?
items.e: Find 2 on the number line and count the X’s above it: 5 students.

items.q: How many students have 1 pet or 2 pets?
items.e: 1 pet: 7 X’s. 2 pets: 5 X’s. 7 + 5 = 12. (3 adds the numbers 1 + 2 on the line.)

items.q: How many more students have 1 pet than 3 pets?
items.e: 1 pet: 7 students. 3 pets: 2 students. 7 − 2 = 5. (2 takes away the numbers on the line: 3 − 1.)

items.q: Kai asks 6 more students. Each of them has 3 pets. How many X’s will be above 3 now?
items.e: There are 2 X’s above 3 now. Add one X for each new student: 2 + 6 = 8.

items.q: In this line plot, what does each X stand for?
items.e: The line plot shows how many teeth each student has lost. Each X is one student, put above the number of teeth that student lost.

items.q: Owen makes a line plot of the letters in his friends’ names: Liam 4, Emma 4, Kai 3, Zoe 3, Owen 4, Mateo 5. How many X’s go above 4?
items.e: Liam, Emma and Owen have 4 letters. That is 3 names, so 3 X’s go above 4. (4 is the number on the line, and 6 is all the names.)

sets.title: Bar graphs (scale of 1) and the mode

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers up the side: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Each line is 1 more, so the scale counts by 1s.

items.q: How many students chose hockey?
items.e: Go to the top of the Hockey bar, then across to the scale. It ends on the line for 8.

items.q: Which bar shows 6 students?
items.e: Find 6 on the scale and go across. The Skating bar ends on the line for 6.

items.q: How many more students chose sledding than skiing?
items.e: Sledding 11, skiing 4. How many more means take away: 11 − 4 = 7. (15 adds them.)

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The mode is the answer chosen most often. The tallest bar is Sledding, so the mode is sledding. 11 is how many students chose it. 11 is not the mode.

items.q: How many students voted altogether?
items.e: Read every bar: 8, 6, 11 and 4. 8 + 6 + 11 + 4 = 29. (4 is the number of bars.)

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: Apple and grapes both have 7 votes, the most. Two bars are tallest and the same height, so this data has two modes: apple and grapes.

items.q: How many fewer students chose orange than banana?
items.e: Banana 5, orange 3. How many fewer means take away: 5 − 3 = 2. (8 adds them.)

items.q: Kai scored these goals in 5 hockey games: 4, 1, 4, 6, 2. What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the number that appears most often. 4 appears two times. The other numbers appear once. The mode is 4. (6 is the biggest number, not the mode.)

items.q: Mitts lost at recess each day: 3, 5, 2, 5, 3, 1. What is the mode?
items.e: 3 appears two times and 5 appears two times. No number appears more often. So there are two modes: 3 and 5.

items.q: Which set of data has no mode?
items.e: In 2, 4, 6, 8 every number appears only once, so there is no mode. 2, 4, 4, 8 has mode 4. 1, 1, 3, 5 has mode 1. 6, 3, 6, 3 has two modes, 3 and 6.

items.q: Which set of data has a mode of 6?
items.e: In 6, 2, 6, 9 the number 6 appears two times, so the mode is 6. The others have modes 9, 1 and 8.

items.q: A good bar graph has a title, labels, a scale and a source. What is missing here?
items.e: There is a scale (0, 1, 2 …), labels (Animal and Votes) and a source under the graph. There is no title at the top. A good title is “Favourite Canadian animal”.

items.q: Where did the data in this bar graph come from?
items.e: The source is written under the graph: “Source: Grade 2 class vote”. The source tells where the data came from.

items.q: Pets in our class: dog 6, cat 4, fish 2, bird 3. Which bar graph shows this data?
items.e: Check each bar against the numbers: dog 6, cat 4, fish 2, bird 3. C matches every number. A: one bar is 1 too tall; B: two bars are the wrong way round; D: one bar is 1 too short.

items.q: Which list matches the bar graph? The order is Noah, Emma, Aiden, Zoe.
items.e: Read each bar against the scale: Noah 9, Emma 12, Aiden 7, Zoe 10.

items.q: How many apples did Noah and Zoe pick altogether?
items.e: Noah 9, Zoe 10. Altogether means add: 9 + 10 = 19. (1 takes away.)

items.q: How many more apples did Emma pick than Aiden?
items.e: Emma 12, Aiden 7. How many more means take away: 12 − 7 = 5. (19 adds them.)

items.q: Zoe picks 3 more apples. Where will the top of her bar be now?
items.e: Zoe’s bar is at 10 now. 3 more: 10 + 3 = 13. (The scale would need to go up to 13.)

items.q: Every bar in a bar graph is the same height. What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the answer that appears most often. If every answer appears the same number of times, no answer is chosen more often, so there is no mode.

items.q: How many students are in this survey?
items.e: Each student answered once. Add every bar: 9 + 12 + 7 + 3 = 31. (12 is only the tallest bar. 4 is the number of bars.)

items.q: Which sentence is true?
c: The bus has 2 more students than walk.
More students walk than come by car.
items.e: Walk 9 and car 7: 9 is more than 7, so this is true. The mode is bus (the tallest bar). Bus has 12 − 9 = 3 more, not 2. 9 is not half of 31.

items.q: The school wants fewer cars. If 4 car students start to walk, how many students will walk?
items.e: 9 students walk now. 4 more will walk: 9 + 4 = 13. (3 is how many will still come by car.)

items.q: What question did the class ask?
c: How do you get to school?
items.e: The bars are ways to get to school: walk, bus, car and bike. Each student answered “How do you get to school?”

items.q: Arjun says, “Most students in Canada take the bus to school.” Is he right?
c: No. The data is from one class.
Yes. Bus has the tallest bar.
No. Walk has the tallest bar.
items.e: The source says the data is from Ms. Lee’s class. It tells us about this class only, not every student in Canada.

items.q: The class will make one dessert. Which one will make the most students happy?
items.e: Pumpkin pie has the longest row: 8 students. It is the mode, so most students will be happy with it.

items.q: How many students did not choose pumpkin pie?
items.e: Add the other rows: 6 + 4 + 6 = 16. (24 is everyone. 10 forgets the apple pie row.)

items.q: 5 more students vote for butter tarts. What is the mode now?
items.e: Butter tarts now has 4 + 5 = 9 votes. 9 is more than 8 (pumpkin pie), so butter tarts is the new mode.

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The tallest stack of X’s is above 6. So 6 laps is the mode. (5 is how many students ran 6 laps. 8 is the biggest number.)

items.q: How many students ran more than 6 laps?
items.e: More than 6 means 7 or 8 laps: 3 + 2 = 5 students. (10 also counts the students who ran 6.)

items.q: The goal was at least 5 laps. How many students ran fewer than 5 laps?
items.e: Fewer than 5 means 3 or 4 laps: 1 + 3 = 4 students. (8 also counts the students who ran 5.)

items.q: How many students ran 4 or 5 laps?
items.e: 4 laps: 3 X’s. 5 laps: 4 X’s. 3 + 4 = 7. (9 adds the numbers 4 + 5 on the line.)

items.q: Mei wants to find out the favourite fruit of her class. Which question should she ask?
items.e: Her question must ask each student for their favourite fruit. “Do you like apples?” only tells her about apples.

items.q: Ethan wants to know which birds come to the school feeder. What is the best way to collect the data?
items.e: He can find out by watching. He makes one tally mark for each bird he sees at the feeder. A favourite bird is not the same as a bird that comes to the feeder.

items.q: Kai asks 10 Grade 1 students and 10 Grade 2 students, “Do you like snow?” 8 Grade 1 students and 6 Grade 2 students say yes. How many students say no?
items.e: 20 students answered. 8 + 6 = 14 say yes. 20 − 14 = 6 say no. (Grade 1: 10 − 8 = 2. Grade 2: 10 − 6 = 4. 2 + 4 = 6.)

items.q: For the food drive, Zoe’s class collected 15 cans in week 1, 22 cans in week 2 and 30 cans in week 3. How many cans did they collect?
items.e: Add all three weeks. 15 + 22 = 37. Then 37 + 30 = 67 cans. (37, 52 and 45 add only two of the weeks.)

items.q: The class wanted 80 cans. They collected 67 cans. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: 80 − 67: count up from 67 to 70 (3), then 70 to 80 (10). 3 + 10 = 13 cans. (27 takes 0 from 7 in the ones place instead of 7 from 0. 3 stops counting at 70.)

items.q: How many more students take the bus than ride a bike?
items.e: Bus 12, bike 3. How many more means take away: 12 − 3 = 9. (15 adds them.)

items.q: Owen says, “Bike is the mode, because it is the shortest bar.” What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the answer chosen most often, so look for the tallest bar. The tallest bar is Bus (12 students). The mode is bus, not the number 12.

items.q: This survey was done in June. The class does it again in January. Why might fewer students ride a bike?
c: Snow and ice make biking hard.
items.e: In January, Ontario has snow and ice, so fewer students bike. When we explain data, we think about when and where it was collected.
